opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the biggest strength of simulation really comes down to one word: scale. In robotics, unlike language models, we don't have the internet as a giant pool of data to scrape. For LLMs, people have been writing text and uploading it for decades, so there's this massive fossil fuel of data just sitting there. For robots, the data we need is continuous control signals, joint angles, motor torques, and nobody is putting that on the internet. You can't just download it.

So the traditional way is teleoperation, where a human operator wears a VR headset or uses some kind of puppeteering rig and controls the robot to collect demonstrations. That's very high quality data, but it's fundamentally limited by 24 hours per robot per day, and in practice much less, because humans get tired and robots break down. It's expensive and slow.

Simulation breaks that bottleneck. In simulation you can run physics at 10,000 times faster than real time, and you can spin up thousands of environments in parallel on a single GPU. So you can compress what would be years of real-world experience into a couple of hours of wall-clock time. That's something you just cannot get any other way.

The second big strength is diversity. In simulation you can do what we call domain randomization: you randomize the gravity, the friction, the mass of objects, the lighting, the textures, the camera angles. And the intuition is that if a neural network can learn to master a thousand different simulated worlds, then the real world just looks like the thousand-and-first one, and it generalizes. That's how we've gotten things like zero-shot sim-to-real transfer, where you train entirely in simulation and deploy directly on the physical robot without any fine-tuning. We've seen this work really well for locomotion, for walking, for dexterous hand manipulation.

And the third piece, which I'm really excited about going forward, is that simulation itself is becoming more generative. Classically, you had to have a team of graphics artists hand-build every asset and every scene, which doesn't scale either. But now we can use generative models to create the 3D assets, the textures, even the layouts and the tasks themselves. And beyond that, video generation models are starting to act as a kind of neural simulation, learned world models that hallucinate plausible futures. Those aren't as precise as a classical physics engine, but they're much more diverse and they capture things that are really hard to hand-code.

So the way I think about it is a data pyramid. At the top you have real robot data: small, expensive, but highest quality and no sim-to-real gap. At the bottom you have internet-scale data like human videos, which is huge and gives you common sense and priors, but it doesn't have the action labels. And in the middle you have simulation and synthetic data, which bridges the two. It has the action labels and it scales with compute instead of with human hours. I think the winning recipe is to mix all three, and simulation is the piece that lets us turn compute into data. That's ultimately what's going to let robotics follow the same kind of scaling story that we've seen in language.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that robotics has a data problem that language models never had. For LLMs, the internet is basically a giant pre-collected dataset of human thought. For robots, there is no internet of physical actions. Every demonstration you collect in the real world costs you a human operator, a physical robot, and real wall-clock time. Robots break, batteries die, you can only run at one-x speed. So real-world data collection is fundamentally bottlenecked by physics and by human labor.

Simulation flips that equation. The first big strength is scale. In a simulator like Isaac, you are not bound to real time. You can run thousands of environments in parallel on a single GPU and compress what would be years of robot experience into a few hours. That is how we trained things like Eureka and the humanoid locomotion work. The policy sees more falls, more slips, more weird contact situations in one night than a physical robot would see in its entire lifetime.

The second strength is diversity. In the real world, you get the lab you have. In simulation, you can randomize everything. Friction, mass, lighting, textures, object shapes, where the camera sits, how much the motors lag. We call this domain randomization. The idea is that if the policy has seen ten thousand slightly different worlds, then the real world just looks like world number ten thousand and one. You are essentially training the robot to be robust to the sim-to-real gap by making the gap itself part of the training distribution.

The third strength, which I think people underrate, is that simulation gives you privileged information. You know the exact ground truth state of every object, you can reset instantly, you can compute dense rewards that would be impossible to measure with real sensors. And now with large language models in the loop, you can even have the model write the reward functions and the task variations for you. That is what Eureka was about. The LLM proposes reward code, the simulator runs it at massive scale, and you close the loop. That kind of automated curriculum is only possible when your environment is software.

Now, I want to be honest that simulation is not free. The gap is real, especially for contact-rich manipulation, deformables, fluids, anything where the physics engine is approximating hard. Rendering is still not photorealistic enough that vision policies transfer cleanly without extra tricks. So in my view the right recipe is a pyramid. At the bottom, enormous amounts of simulation data and internet video for breadth. In the middle, synthetic data that is augmented or generated by models. And at the top, a thin layer of real robot demonstrations to ground everything. Simulation is what makes the bottom of that pyramid wide enough that the top layer can actually generalize.

r002.rationale: It says simulation is not bound to real time and can compress years of robot experience into a few hours.

astra-6.text:
The biggest strength is scale. With a real robot, collecting data is limited by physical time: you have to run the experiment, reset the scene, and deal with wear and tear. In simulation, you can have thousands of robots practicing in parallel, and you can expose them to situations that would be expensive or dangerous to create in the real world.

You also control the environment. You can vary the lighting, friction, object shapes, and sensor noise, so the robot learns to handle a range of conditions instead of memorizing one setup. And you have access to ground truth—where every object is and what’s happening at each step.

The challenge is transferring that learning to reality. A simulator is never a perfect model of the world. But it doesn’t necessarily need to be. If you train across enough variation, the real world can become another variation the robot knows how to handle. That’s the promise: turning compute into useful physical experience.

sol-6.1.text:
The biggest strength is that simulation lets you scale experience. A robot in the real world has to collect data in real time. In simulation, you can run thousands of environments in parallel, let robots try things, fail, and try again without breaking hardware or putting anyone at risk.

And you control the world. You can change the lighting, the friction, the mass of an object, or the layout of a room. Instead of learning one very specific setup, the robot can train across a wide range of conditions. You also have access to the underlying state of the simulation, so you can get labels that would be difficult or expensive to obtain in the real world.

The challenge is transferring that learning to a physical robot. Simulation is always an approximation. But if you build enough useful variation into training, the real world can start to look like another variation the robot knows how to handle.
